headline: Android 17 QPR2 Beta 3 adds new customization and security features, public rollout in Dec.
summary: Google's latest Android 17 QPR2 Beta 3 introduces enhanced Quick Settings layout editing, more precise theming options, and expanded blur effects, alongside new security restrictions for call forwarding.
details: Google has rolled out the third beta of Android 17 QPR2 to users on the public beta program. This update includes notable bug fixes and several new features, with the public release anticipated in December this year.

A key highlight of this beta release is a set of new security restrictions. These measures focus on programmatic call forwarding to better protect users from potential frauds and unauthorized activities.

Users will gain more control over their device interface with a new Quick Settings layout editor. This feature allows for flexible placement of Quick Settings tiles, including moving the brightness slider and media player to the bottom for easier access.

The beta also expands theming options, introducing a new slider. This slider enables fine-tuning of the hue and four main color styles, offering greater customization over the overall look and feel of the Android UI.

Furthermore, blur effects have been expanded to cover more interface elements. These now include lock screen shortcuts, the fingerprint button, and notifications, enhancing the visual consistency and depth of the system.

The new beta builds are currently rolling out via OTA to users in the Public Preview program. Additionally, images are available for download on Google's website for all compatible devices, starting with the Pixel 6a.

headline_marked: [[AI could make software too secure]], causing law enforcement to 'go dark'
headline: AI could make software too secure, causing law enforcement to 'go dark'
summary: New AI models are becoming exceptionally skilled at finding software vulnerabilities, potentially making systems impenetrable and causing law enforcement agencies to lose their ability to access crucial data.
details: The rapid advancement of AI in finding software vulnerabilities is raising concerns that it could inadvertently make systems too secure, leading to a new era where law enforcement agencies struggle to access crucial digital evidence.

This phenomenon, dubbed 'going dark,' refers to the potential loss of investigative capabilities for intelligence and law enforcement agencies as digital communications become increasingly encrypted and secure.

The shift began in the late 2000s with smartphones and texting, moving away from easily wiretapped calls. By 2010, Apple began encrypting iPhone storage, followed by Android, and end-to-end encryption became standard in apps like iMessage and WhatsApp by 2016.
In response, the FBI launched its 'Going Dark' initiative in 2014, seeking a national conversation on how providers could be compelled to make communications legible to law enforcement.

A key moment was the 2016 Apple v. FBI case, where Apple refused to unlock a terrorist's iPhone. The stalemate was broken not by Apple's compliance, but by an outside company successfully hacking the device.

For the next decade, law enforcement and intelligence agencies continued to seek 'exceptional access' backdoors, but increasingly relied on purchasing targeted hacking tools like GrayKey for phone unlocking or NSO Group's Pegasus for remote exploitation.

However, a new paradigm is emerging with AI models. In April, Anthropic announced Mythos, a model unusually skilled at finding software vulnerabilities, prompting a temporary export block by the U.S. government.

Other labs, including OpenAI and Chinese open-weight model developers like Z.ai and Moonshot, have also demonstrated significant capabilities in vulnerability finding. This widespread AI proficiency could soon make software genuinely too secure for traditional hacking methods, ending the era of purchasable exploits.
